Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first
argument ([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A,B$ be
symmetric densely defined operators on $\mathcal H$
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]), and let
$u\in D(A)\cap D(B)$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Put
$$a:=\langle Au,u\rangle,\quad b:=\langle Bu,u\rangle,\quad x:=(A-a)u,\quad y:=(B-b)u,\quad \Delta A:=\|x\|,\quad\Delta B:=\|y\|,$$
and define the **covariance** of the pair $(A,B)$ in the preparation $u$ by
$\operatorname{Cov}_u(A,B):=\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle$.
Then:

(a) $a,b\in\mathbb R$; $x,y\in\mathcal H$; and
$\operatorname{Cov}_u(A,B)\in\mathbb R$ is symmetric in its two arguments:
$\operatorname{Cov}_u(A,B)=\operatorname{Cov}_u(B,A)$;

(b) *covariance-refined bound:*
$$(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}_u(A,B)\bigr]^2 +\bigl[\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle\bigr]^2 \ge\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}_u(A,B)\bigr]^2,$$
so in particular $\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge|\operatorname{Cov}_u(A,B)|$;

(c) equality holds in (b)'s first inequality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are
linearly dependent (in the convention that $x=0$ or $y=0$ counts as
dependence);

(d) if in addition $u\in D(AB)\cap D(BA)$ — that is $Bu\in D(A)$ and
$Au\in D(B)$ — then the pairing
$\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle:=\langle ABu,u\rangle-\langle BAu,u\rangle$ is
defined and
$$\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle=-2i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle,$$
in particular it is purely imaginary, and consequently
$$(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}_u(A,B)\bigr]^2 +\tfrac14\bigl|\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle\bigr|^2, \qquad \Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\tfrac12\bigl|\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle\bigr| .$$

Clauses (a)-(c) use no product $AB$ or $BA$ and no assumption on the domains
of such products. The quantities are preparation quantities of the vector $u$;
no measurement model, apparatus error or energy-time interpretation is
asserted.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

derivations.claim: [Means and centered vectors] By [F1] the numbers $a$ and $b$ are real and $x=(A-a)u$, $y=(B-b)u$ lie in $H$, so $\Delta A=\|x\|$ and $\Delta B=\|y\|$ are the norms of the centered vectors.

[The real part is the anticommutator pairing] Since $Bu\in D(A)$ and $Au\in D(B)$, symmetry of $A$ gives $\langle ABu,u\rangle=\langle Bu,Au\rangle=\overline{\langle Au,Bu\rangle}$ and symmetry of $B$ gives $\langle BAu,u\rangle=\langle Au,Bu\rangle$. Adding, $\langle\{A,B\}u,u\rangle=2\operatorname{Re}\langle Au,Bu\rangle$. By [F2], $\langle x,y\rangle=\langle Au,Bu\rangle-ab$ with $ab\in\mathbb R$, hence $\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{Re}\langle Au,Bu\rangle-ab=\tfrac12\langle\{A,B\}u,u\rangle-ab$. Expanding the anticommutator of the centered operators, using $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $\langle Au,u\rangle=a$, $\langle Bu,u\rangle=b$, gives $\langle\{(A-a),(B-b)\}u,u\rangle=\langle\{A,B\}u,u\rangle-2ab$, so the two displays for the real part agree.

[The imaginary part is the commutator pairing] By [F2], $\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle=-2i\operatorname{Im}\langle Au,Bu\rangle$; by step 2.1 and [F2], $\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{Im}\langle Au,Bu\rangle$, so $\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle=-2i\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle$. This completes (a).

[The two bounds] By [F1] the refined bound $(\Delta A)^{2}(\Delta B)^{2}\ge[\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle]^{2}+[\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle]^{2}$ holds. Substituting step 2.1 and $|\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle|=\tfrac12|\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle|$ from step 3.1 gives (c); dropping the nonnegative first square gives (b).
[Equality] By [F1] equality in the refined bound holds if and only if $x,y$ are linearly dependent; this is (d).

[Bounded case] If $A$ and $B$ are bounded everywhere-defined self-adjoint operators then $D(A)=D(B)=H$ and all products are everywhere defined, so the product-domain hypothesis of the statement holds for every unit $u\in H$ by [F4]; the displays of (a)-(d) are then unconditional in $u$. This is (e).

boundaries.reason: The statement concerns two operators and one unit vector; no empty family, empty sum or empty index set occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 allows the centered vector $x=0$ or $y=0$; step 4.1 then gives the bounds with both sides zero, and step 5.1 treats the vanishing vector as linearly dependent.
Step 6.1 covers the single-term case of bounded operators, and steps 1.1-5.1 are uniform in the pair, so the one-operator case $A=B$ is included.
Step 1.1 allows degenerate centered vectors; step 5.1 records the linear-dependence convention that covers them.

boundaries.reason: No interval endpoint, boundary value or limit at infinity is asserted; all pairings are finite by the stated domain hypotheses.
Only the Axiom of Countable Choice for the Hilbert-space and integral conventions is assumed; no family of nonempty sets is selected.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 proves that linear dependence of the centered vectors yields equality in the refined bound.
Step 5.1 proves conversely that equality in the refined bound forces linear dependence.

risk_review.notes: All six steps checked against weak Robertson, covariance-refined inequality and Cauchy-Schwarz exact statements. Product-domain membership licenses both symmetry pairings. First-variable linearity gives commutator -2i Im and anticommutator 2 Re; real means give centered pairing minus ab. Equality iff linear dependence includes either zero centered vector, and bounded full-domain case satisfies both products. Zero Hilbert space has no unit vector. Countable Choice explicitly inherited. No physical or energy-time conclusion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and for a bounded measurable $f$ write $\Phi_E(f)=\int f\,dE$ for
the operator of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]. Then:

1. $\Phi_E$ is linear and unital: $\Phi_E(\mathbf 1_X)=I$ and
   $\Phi_E(af+bg)=a\Phi_E(f)+b\Phi_E(g)$ for bounded measurable $f,g$ and
   $a,b\in\mathbb C$;
2. $\Phi_E$ is multiplicative: $\Phi_E(fg)=\Phi_E(f)\Phi_E(g)$;
3. $\Phi_E$ preserves conjugation: $\Phi_E(\overline f)=\Phi_E(f)^*$;
4. if $(f_n)$ are bounded measurable with $\sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty$, $f$
   is bounded measurable, and $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere,
   meaning $E_x$-almost everywhere for every $x\in H$, then
   $\Phi_E(f_n)\to\Phi_E(f)$ in the strong operator topology.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X$ be LCH and suppose every open subset of $X$ is sigma-compact. Every Borel measure finite on compact sets is regular: it is outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular by compact sets on every Borel set.
For $n\ge1$, Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is locally compact and $\sigma$-compact.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $p, q \in X$ with
$p \ne q$. Put $r := d(p,q)/2$. Then $r > 0$ and

$$B(p,r) \cap B(q,r) = \emptyset .$$

Both sets are open ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]) and contain $p$
respectively $q$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), so every metric space is **Hausdorff**:
distinct points are separated by disjoint open sets
([[def-metric-topology]]).

Every open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a countable union of intervals $(a,b)$
with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$ and $a<b$. For $U=\varnothing$, the indexing family is
empty.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: [Simple functions commute] Let $f=\sum_{i}a_{i}\mathbf 1_{\Lambda_{i}}$ and $g=\sum_{j}b_{j}\mathbf 1_{\Sigma_{j}}$ be complex simple Borel functions over disjoint measurable covers. By [F1], $f(A)=\sum_{i}a_{i}E_{A}(\Lambda_{i})$ and $g(B)=\sum_{j}b_{j}E_{B}(\Sigma_{j})$, so $f(A)g(B)=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}E_{A}(\Lambda_{i})E_{B}(\Sigma_{j})=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}E_{B}(\Sigma_{j})E_{A}(\Lambda_{i})=g(B)f(A),$ because products of scalars commute and each pair of projections commutes by the strong commutation hypothesis.

[Uniform approximation] Let $f,g$ be bounded Borel and fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F4] choose simple $s,t$ with $\|f-s\|_{\infty}\le\varepsilon$ and $\|g-t\|_{\infty}\le\varepsilon$. By [F1], $\|s(A)-f(A)\|\le\varepsilon$, $\|t(B)-g(B)\|\le\varepsilon$ and $\|t(B)\|\le\|g\|_{\infty}+\varepsilon$, so the operator norm estimate $\|s(A)t(B)-f(A)g(B)\|\le\|s(A)-f(A)\|\,\|t(B)\|+\|f(A)\|\,\|t(B)-g(B)\|\le\varepsilon\bigl(\|g\|_{\infty}+\varepsilon+\|f\|_{\infty}\bigr)$ gives $s(A)t(B)\to f(A)g(B)$ in operator norm as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, with the approximants chosen along any sequence $\varepsilon_{n}\to0$.

[Clause (a)] Let $f,g$ be bounded Borel and choose the approximating sequences $s_{n}\to f$, $t_{n}\to g$ of step 1.2. By step 1.1, $s_{n}(A)t_{n}(B)=t_{n}(B)s_{n}(A)$ for every $n$; both sides converge in operator norm to $f(A)g(B)$ and to $g(B)f(A)$ respectively by step 1.2 (applied to the pairs $(s_{n},t_{n})$ and $(t_{n},s_{n})$). Limits in operator norm are unique, so $f(A)g(B)=g(B)f(A)$. This is (a).

[Clause (c), first part] Let $f$ be bounded Borel and let $\Lambda$ be Borel. Applying (a), already proved, to the bounded Borel function $\mathbf 1_{\Lambda}$ of $A$ and $f$ of $B$ gives $E_{A}(\Lambda)f(B)=f(B)E_{A}(\Lambda)$. This is the first assertion of (c).

[Clause (b), membership in the domain] Fix a bounded Borel $f$ and $x\in D(A)$; put $y:=f(B)x$. Put $u_{n}(\lambda):=\lambda\mathbf 1_{\{|\lambda|\le n\}}$, so that $A_{n}=\int u_{n}\,dE_{A}$ is a bounded Borel function of $A$; clause (a), already proved, applied to the pair of bounded Borel functions $(u_{n},f)$ gives $A_{n}f(B)=f(B)A_{n}$, so by [F1] and [F3] $\int\lambda^{2}\mathbf 1_{\{|\lambda|\le n\}}\,dE_{A,y}=\|A_{n}y\|^{2}=\|A_{n}f(B)x\|^{2}=\|f(B)A_{n}x\|^{2}\le\|f(B)\|^{2}\|A_{n}x\|^{2}\le\|f(B)\|^{2}\|Ax\|^{2},$ where the last step uses $\|A_{n}x\|\le\|Ax\|$ for $x\in D(A)$. Letting $n\to\infty$ and using monotone convergence on the left (equivalently the identities of [F3]) gives $\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,y}\le\|f(B)\|^{2}\|Ax\|^{2}<\infty$, so $y\in D(A)$.

[Clause (b), action] With $x$ and $y=f(B)x$ as in step 4.1, both $x$ and $y$ lie in $D(A)$. By [F3], $A_{n}x\to Ax$ and $A_{n}y\to Ay$. Using $A_{n}f(B)=f(B)A_{n}$ from step 4.1, $Ay=\lim_{n}A_{n}y=\lim_{n}A_{n}f(B)x=\lim_{n}f(B)A_{n}x=f(B)Ax,$ the last equality because $f(B)$ is bounded and $A_{n}x\to Ax$. Hence $Af(B)x=f(B)Ax$ for every $x\in D(A)$. Exchanging the roles of $A$ and $B$ gives the other asserted identity, since the strong commutation hypothesis is symmetric.

[Norm limits of functions of $B$] Let $T_n$ be a sequence of bounded Borel functions of $B$ that converges in operator norm to a bounded operator $T$. By steps 4.1-5.1, for every $x\in D(A)$ one has $T_nx\in D(A)$ and $AT_nx=T_nAx$. Thus $T_nx\to Tx$ and $AT_nx=T_nAx\to T Ax$. Since the self-adjoint operator $A$ is closed, $Tx\in D(A)$ and $ATx=T Ax$. Finite bounded linear combinations are again bounded Borel functions of $B$, so the same domain and action identities hold for them. This completes (b).

[Clause (c), composition] Let $f$ be real-valued and bounded Borel and put $F(\Lambda):=E_{A}(f^{-1}(\Lambda))$ for Borel $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R$. Preimages preserve the empty set, the whole space, complements and countable unions, so $F$ is a projection-valued measure. Each $F_x$ is a finite positive Borel measure, hence finite on compact sets, and is regular by [F5]; thus $F$ is a regular PVM. For a complex simple $u=\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathbf 1_{D_{i}}$ the preimages $f^{-1}(D_{i})$ are pairwise disjoint, so $\int u\,dF=\sum_{i}c_{i}F(D_{i})=\sum_{i}c_{i}E_{A}(f^{-1}(D_{i}))=\int(u\circ f)\,dE_{A}$; both sides extend to bounded Borel $u$ by the uniform approximation of [F1] and [F4], giving, for every $x\in H$, the scalar identity $\int u\,dF_{x}=\int(u\circ f)\,dE_{A,x}$. Taking $u(\lambda)=v_n(\lambda):=\lambda^2\mathbf1_{\{|\lambda|\le n\}}$ and letting $n\to\infty$ by [F6] gives $\int\lambda^{2}\,dF_{x}=\int f^{2}\,dE_{A,x}=\|f(A)x\|^{2}<\infty$, where the last equality is [F1] for the bounded $f$; and, choosing $R>\|f\|_\infty$, $F(\mathbb R\setminus[-R,R])=0$, so applying the operator identity to $u(\lambda)=\lambda\mathbf1_{[-R,R]}(\lambda)$ gives $\int\lambda\,dF_{x,y}=\int f\,dE_{A,x,y}=\langle f(A)x,y\rangle$ for all $x,y\in H$. Since $f$ is real-valued, the adjoint-preservation clause of [F2] gives $f(A)^{*}=\Phi_{E_{A}}(\overline f)=\Phi_{E_{A}}(f)=f(A)$, so $f(A)$ is self-adjoint, and $f(A)$ is bounded by [F1]. By the uniqueness of the spectral projection-valued measure of a self-adjoint operator in [F3], $F$ is the spectral projection-valued measure of the bounded self-adjoint operator $f(A)$. By the strong commutation hypothesis, $F(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)=E_{A}(f^{-1}(\Lambda))E_{B}(\Sigma)=E_{B}(\Sigma)E_{A}(f^{-1}(\Lambda))=E_{B}(\Sigma)F(\Lambda)$, so $(f(A),B)$ strongly commutes. Applying the same argument once more, now to the pair $(f(A),B)$ and the real-valued bounded Borel function $g$, shows that $(f(A),g(B))$ strongly commutes. This completes (c).

**(a) Setting.** Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of
the spectral theorem. Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $A$ and $B$ be self-adjoint operators on $H$
with domains $D(A)$ and $D(B)$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). By the spectral
theorem each of them has a unique spectral projection-valued measure on the
Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]); write $E_{A}$
for the spectral projection-valued measure of $A$ and $E_{B}$ for that of $B$.

**(b) Strong spectral commutation.** The operators $A$ and $B$ **strongly
commute**, or are **spectrally compatible**, when their spectral
projection-valued measures commute on every pair of Borel sets:
$$E_{A}(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)=E_{B}(\Sigma)E_{A}(\Lambda)\qquad\text{for all Borel }\Lambda,\Sigma\subseteq\mathbb R .$$
This is the relation that the term "compatible sharp observables" abbreviates
on the physical pages of the category. It is a condition on the two families
of projections, not on a single vector or on a formal difference of operator
products.

**(c) Not to be confused with a commutator identity on a dense invariant
domain.** Let $D$ be a dense linear subspace of $D(A)\cap D(B)$ such that
$AD\subseteq D$ and $BD\subseteq D$. Then $ABu$ and $BAu$ are defined for every
$u\in D$. Strong spectral commutation implies $ABu=BAu$ on $D$: Teschl's
bounded Borel calculus for a strongly commuting pair gives, for each bounded
Borel function $h$, $h(B)D(A)\subseteq D(A)$ and $Ah(B)x=h(B)Ax$ for
$x\in D(A)$ (Section 4.2, Lemma 4.5). Apply this with
$h_n(\lambda)=\lambda\mathbf 1_{[-n,n]}(\lambda)$. For $u\in D$, both $u$ and
$Au$ belong to $D(B)$, so the spectral theorem gives $h_n(B)u\to Bu$ and
$h_n(B)Au\to BAu$. Since $Ah_n(B)u=h_n(B)Au$ and $A$ is closed, it follows
that $Bu\in D(A)$ and $ABu=BAu$. The converse can fail even for a dense
common invariant domain: the examples page records a pair of self-adjoint
extensions for which the commutator vanishes on such a domain but the spectral
projections do not commute.

For bounded everywhere-defined self-adjoint $A$ and $B$, if the commutator
vanishes on a dense $D$, boundedness extends $AB=BA$ to all of $H$; the bounded
Borel calculus then makes this equivalent to strong spectral commutation
(Teschl, Section 4.2, Corollary 4.7). No graph-norm core property is needed in
the comparison above. Clause (b), rather than a domain commutator identity, is
the definition governing joint sharp outcomes.

**(d) Status.** Clauses (a)-(c) fix a definition and a comparison of
conditions. They assert no physical claim, no joint measurement, no
simultaneous sharp value and no dynamical statement. All further content about
strong spectral commutation used by the category -- the bounded-calculus
consequences, the joint projection-valued measure criterion and the physical
readings -- is established as separate results with their own hypotheses.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero
complex Hilbert space and let $A,B$ be self-adjoint operators on $H$ with
spectral projection-valued measures $E_{A},E_{B}$ that strongly commute in the
sense of [[def-nrqm-uncertainty-strong-spectral-commutation]] clause (b):
$$E_{A}(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)=E_{B}(\Sigma)E_{A}(\Lambda)\qquad\text{for all Borel }\Lambda,\Sigma\subseteq\mathbb R .$$
For a bounded Borel function $h$ write $h(A):=\int h\,dE_{A}$ and
$h(B):=\int h\,dE_{B}$ for its operators under the bounded Borel functional
calculus ([[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]). Then:

(a) for all bounded Borel $f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$,
$$f(A)g(B)=g(B)f(A);$$

(b) for every bounded Borel $f$ one has $f(B)D(A)\subseteq D(A)$, and
$$A\,f(B)x=f(B)Ax\qquad\text{for every }x\in D(A);$$
the same statement holds with the roles of $A$ and $B$ exchanged, and it is
also true with $f(B)$ replaced by any bounded linear combination or norm limit
of bounded Borel functions of $B$;

(c) for every bounded Borel $f$ the bounded operator $f(B)$ commutes with all
spectral projections of $A$: $f(B)E_{A}(\Lambda)=E_{A}(\Lambda)f(B)$ for every
Borel $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R$. Consequently, for real-valued bounded Borel
$f$ the pair $(f(A),B)$ strongly commutes: the map
$F(\Lambda):=E_{A}(f^{-1}(\Lambda))$ is a projection-valued measure on the
Borel sets of $\mathbb R$ representing the bounded self-adjoint operator
$f(A)$, and $F(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)=E_{B}(\Sigma)F(\Lambda)$ for all Borel
$\Lambda,\Sigma$; hence also $(f(A),g(B))$ strongly commutes for real-valued
bounded Borel $f,g$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $E,F$ be **regular** projection-valued measures on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) satisfying the strong commutation relation

$$E(B)F(C)=F(C)E(B)\qquad\text{for all Borel }B,C\subseteq\mathbb R .$$

Then there is a unique regular projection-valued measure $G$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R^2$ with

$$G(B\times C)=E(B)F(C)\qquad\text{for every Borel rectangle }B\times C,$$

where rectangle means a measurable rectangle in the sense of [[def-measurable-rectangle]]. Its marginals are $G(B\times\mathbb R)=E(B)$ and $G(\mathbb R\times C)=F(C)$.

For the scalar construction, let $\mathcal A_0$ be the algebra of finite unions of Borel rectangles, and define $P_0(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^n B_i\times C_i):=\sum_{i=1}^nE(B_i)F(C_i)$ on disjoint rectangular decompositions. For every $\psi\in H$, $\mu_\psi(A):=\langle P_0(A)\psi,\psi\rangle$ is a finite premeasure on $\mathcal A_0$ and has a unique extension $G_\psi=\langle G(\cdot)\psi,\psi\rangle$ to the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $x,y\in H$, define the polarized measure $\nu_{x,y}:=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^3 i^kG_{x+i^ky}$. Then every Borel $S\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ has a unique bounded operator $G(S)$ satisfying $\langle G(S)x,y\rangle=\nu_{x,y}(S)$ for all $x,y\in H$, and $0\le G(S)\le I$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X$ be LCH and suppose every open subset of $X$ is sigma-compact. Every Borel measure finite on compact sets is regular: it is outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular by compact sets on every Borel set.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and for a bounded measurable $f$ write $\Phi_E(f)=\int f\,dE$ for
the operator of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]. Then:

1. $\Phi_E$ is linear and unital: $\Phi_E(\mathbf 1_X)=I$ and
   $\Phi_E(af+bg)=a\Phi_E(f)+b\Phi_E(g)$ for bounded measurable $f,g$ and
   $a,b\in\mathbb C$;
2. $\Phi_E$ is multiplicative: $\Phi_E(fg)=\Phi_E(f)\Phi_E(g)$;
3. $\Phi_E$ preserves conjugation: $\Phi_E(\overline f)=\Phi_E(f)^*$;
4. if $(f_n)$ are bounded measurable with $\sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty$, $f$
   is bounded measurable, and $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere,
   meaning $E_x$-almost everywhere for every $x\in H$, then
   $\Phi_E(f_n)\to\Phi_E(f)$ in the strong operator topology.

derivations.claim: [(i) implies (ii)] Assume (i). By [F4] the projection-valued measures $E_{A}$ and $E_{B}$ are regular, and by [F1] they commute on all Borel pairs; so [F3] supplies a unique regular projection-valued measure $G$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R^{2}$ with $G(\Lambda\times\Sigma)=E_{A}(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)$ for all measurable rectangles and with the stated marginals. This is (ii), including uniqueness.

[(ii) implies (i)] Assume (ii). For Borel $\Lambda,\Sigma$, the multiplicativity [F5] and the marginals give $$E_{A}(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)=G(\Lambda\times\mathbb R)\,G(\mathbb R\times\Sigma)=G(\Lambda\times\Sigma)=G(\mathbb R\times\Sigma)\,G(\Lambda\times\mathbb R)=E_{B}(\Sigma)E_{A}(\Lambda),$$ using $(\Lambda\times\mathbb R)\cap(\mathbb R\times\Sigma)=\Lambda\times\Sigma$. This is (i).
[(i) implies (iii)] This is [F2] verbatim.
[(iii) implies (i)] Assume (iii). Taking $f=\mathbf 1_{\Lambda}$ and $g=\mathbf 1_{\Sigma}$, which are bounded Borel, gives $E_{A}(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)=E_{B}(\Sigma)E_{A}(\Lambda)$. This is (i).

[The joint representation] Assume (i)-(iii) and let $G$ be the unique joint projection-valued measure of (ii), so that $G(\Lambda\times\Sigma)=E_{A}(\Lambda)E_{B}(\Sigma)$ for rectangles. Let $W(h):=\int h\,dG$ denote the bounded integral against $G$ for bounded Borel $h:\mathbb R^{2}\to\mathbb C$. For simple $s=\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathbf 1_{\Lambda_{i}}$, $t=\sum_{j}d_{j}\mathbf 1_{\Sigma_{j}}$ over disjoint covers of $\mathbb R$, the disjointness of the rectangles $\Lambda_{i}\times\Sigma_{j}$ and the defining property of the simple integral against a projection-valued measure give $$s(A)t(B)=\sum_{i,j}c_{i}d_{j}E_{A}(\Lambda_{i})E_{B}(\Sigma_{j})=\sum_{i,j}c_{i}d_{j}G(\Lambda_{i}\times\Sigma_{j})=W(s\otimes t).$$ For general bounded Borel $f,g$ choose simple $s_{n},t_{n}$ with $\|f-s_{n}\|_{\infty}\to0$ and $\|g-t_{n}\|_{\infty}\to0$ (uniform approximation by preimages of finite Borel partitions of bounded squares in $\mathbb C$, as in [F6]); then $\|s_{n}\otimes t_{n}-f\otimes g\|_{\infty}\to0$, so by the norm bound of [F6] both $s_{n}(A)t_{n}(B)\to f(A)g(B)$ and $W(s_{n}\otimes t_{n})\to W(f\otimes g)$ in operator norm, whence $f(A)g(B)=W(f\otimes g)=\int f(a)g(b)\,dG(a,b)$; combining with [F2] gives the displayed chain.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the
cited scalar operator and spectral suppliers. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$. Let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the
component-valued space of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]
with its componentwise inner product, let $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$ be the
scalar position and momentum operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]], and let
$\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^{1}$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Write
$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}:=\Psi_{0}\bigl(\bigoplus_{l}\mathcal F_{2}\bigr)\Psi_{0}^{-1}$
for its componentwise version, with $\Psi_{0}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a).
Define, componentwise,
$$D(Q_{j}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (Q_{j}f)_{l}:=x_{j}f_{l},$$
$$D(P_{k}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ D_{k}f_{l}\text{ exists in }L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
where $D_{k}$ is the weak derivative of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]].
Write $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the classes whose components
lie in $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]),
and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the componentwise Schwartz
class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]). Then:

(a) under $\Psi_{0}$ the operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are the orthogonal sums
$\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]]; in particular
$Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are densely defined and self-adjoint with the displayed
domains;

(b) $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is unitary,
$$D(P_{k})=\bigl\{f\in H^{(r)}:\ \xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\bigr\},$$
and for every $f\in D(P_{k})$
$$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}(P_{k}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\,\xi_{k}\,\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi;$$

(c) the componentwise translation $T_{a}^{(r)}f:=f(\cdot-a)$, $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$,
is unitary, leaves $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$,
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$
invariant, satisfies $D_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)}f)=T_{a}^{(r)}(D_{k}f)$ for
$f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$, and
$$T_{a}^{(r)}D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=Q_{j}-a_{j}I,\qquad T_{a}^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(P_{k}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}P_{k}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=P_{k};$$

(d) for every $f\in D(P_{j})$,
$$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}f-f\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}f \qquad\text{in }H^{(r)},$$
so the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$t\mapsto T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}$ has generator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$ and
$$T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tP_{j}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the exponential being the spectral-calculus flow of the self-adjoint operator
$P_{j}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix integers $d\ge1$,
$r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$, let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with
the componentwise position and momentum operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]], let
$\mathcal S^{(r)}:=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the componentwise
Schwartz class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]), and let $\Psi_{0}$
and $\Theta$ be the unitaries of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]. For
$S=(S_{lm})\in M_{r}(\mathbb C)$ write
$$S_{\times}f:=\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^{r}S_{lm}f_{m}\Bigr)_{l}\qquad(f\in H^{(r)}).$$
Then:

(a) $\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq D(Q_{j})\cap D(P_{k})$ for all $j,k$,
$Q_{j}\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and
$P_{k}\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq\mathcal S^{(r)}$, and on $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ the
canonical commutation relations hold:
$$(Q_{j}P_{k}-P_{k}Q_{j})f=i\hbar\,\delta_{jk}f\qquad(f\in\mathcal S^{(r)});$$

(b) $S_{\times}$ is bounded with $\|S_{\times}\|=\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}$
([[def-operator-norm]]), and
$$S_{\times}D(Q_{j})\subseteq D(Q_{j}),\quad Q_{j}S_{\times}f=S_{\times}Q_{j}f\ (f\in D(Q_{j})),\qquad S_{\times}D(P_{k})\subseteq D(P_{k}),\quad P_{k}S_{\times}f=S_{\times}P_{k}f\ (f\in D(P_{k}));$$

(c) the spectral projection-valued measures of $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are
$$E_{Q_{j}}(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}},\qquad E_{P_{k}}(B)=\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)*}M_{\mathbf 1_{\{2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\in B\}}}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)} \qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
where $M_{g}$ is multiplication by $g$; consequently
$S_{\times}E_{Q_{j}}(B)=E_{Q_{j}}(B)S_{\times}$ and
$S_{\times}E_{P_{k}}(B)=E_{P_{k}}(B)S_{\times}$ for every Borel $B$, and for
unitary $V\in U(r)$ and every $f\in H^{(r)}$
$$\bigl\|E_{Q_{j}}(B)V_{\times}f\bigr\|=\bigl\|E_{Q_{j}}(B)f\bigr\|,\qquad \bigl\|E_{P_{k}}(B)V_{\times}f\bigr\|=\bigl\|E_{P_{k}}(B)f\bigr\|;$$

(d) under the tensor identification $\Theta$ the operator $S_{\times}$
corresponds to the bounded amplification $I\otimes S$ of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], that is
$\Theta^{-1}S_{\times}\Theta=I\otimes S$; in particular the internal-factor
operators commute with the spatial ones in the sense of (b).

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]

derivations.claim: [The product rule] Let $f\in H^{(r)}$ with $x_{j}f\in L^{2}$ and $x_{j}D_{j}f\in L^{2}$. Componentwise, $f_l\in L^2\subseteq L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by [F4]. The occurrence of $D_jf_l$ in the hypothesis uses the stated locally integrable weak derivative; no global $L^2$ membership of $D_jf_l$ is needed for clause (a). Thus [F2] with $\alpha=e_{j}$ and $\eta=x_{j}$ applies and gives $D_{j}(x_{j}f_{l})=f_{l}+x_{j}D_{j}f_{l}$ in $L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every $l$. The right-hand side is a component of an $L^{2}$ class by hypothesis, so $D_{j}(x_{j}f)\in L^{2}$ componentwise and $x_{j}f\in D(P_{j})$ with the displayed identity. This is (a).

[The two product domains] By [F1], $D(Q_{j}P_{j})=\{f:\ P_{j}f\in D(Q_{j})\}=\{f\in D(P_{j}):\ x_{j}D_{j}f\in L^{2}\}$ and $D(P_{j}Q_{j})=\{f:\ Q_{j}f\in D(P_{j})\}=\{f\in D(Q_{j}):\ D_{j}(x_{j}f)\in L^{2}\}$, which are the first two displays of (b). For the intersection, the inclusion $\subseteq$ is immediate from these displays; conversely, if $f\in H^{(r)}$ has $D_{j}f$, $x_{j}f$ and $x_{j}D_{j}f$ in $L^{2}$, then $f\in D(P_{j})\cap D(Q_{j})$ and step 1.1 gives $D_{j}(x_{j}f)=f+x_{j}D_{j}f\in L^{2}$, so $f$ lies in both product domains. This is (b).

[The commutator] Let $f\in D(Q_{j}P_{j})\cap D(P_{j}Q_{j})$. By [F1] and step 2.1, $(Q_{j}P_{j}f)_{l}=x_{j}(-i\hbar D_{j}f_{l})=-i\hbar\,x_{j}D_{j}f_{l}$ componentwise, while $(P_{j}Q_{j}f)_{l}=-i\hbar D_{j}(x_{j}f_{l})=-i\hbar(f_{l}+x_{j}D_{j}f_{l})$ by step 1.1. Subtracting componentwise, $((Q_{j}P_{j}-P_{j}Q_{j})f)_{l}=-i\hbar x_{j}D_{j}f_{l}+i\hbar f_{l}+i\hbar x_{j}D_{j}f_{l}=i\hbar f_{l}$, so $(Q_{j}P_{j}-P_{j}Q_{j})f=i\hbar f$. This is (c).

[The core] Every component of a Schwartz class lies in the scalar Schwartz class, which is closed under multiplication by $x_{j}$ and under $D_{j}$ and is contained in $L^{2}$; hence $D_{j}f$, $x_{j}f$ and $x_{j}D_{j}f$ are in $L^{2}$, and step 2.1 places $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ in the intersection. The identity of (c), together with [F3], gives (d).

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 verifies the commutator identity for the zero class, both product domains containing it with value zero.
Step 3.1 gives $(Q_{j}P_{j}-P_{j}Q_{j})0=i\hbar\cdot0$; the product rule of step 1.1 also holds for the zero class.
Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 are stated for one coordinate $j$ and uniform in $d$ and $r$, so the case $d=r=1$ is the displayed computation.
Step 2.1 records that $D(P_{j}Q_{j})$ is in general strictly larger than $D(Q_{j}P_{j})$, so the intersection characterization is not reduced to either product domain.

boundaries.reason: The space is $\mathbb R^{d}$ with no boundary or endpoint; no trace or boundary condition enters.
Countable Choice is carried by the weak-derivative and Lebesgue conventions; no family selection occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 proves that the characterized set is contained in both product domains.
Step 2.1 also proves that every element of the two product domains satisfies the three $L^{2}$ memberships, giving the converse inclusion.

risk_review.notes: All four steps and exact componentwise maximal-domain, weak Leibniz and Schwartz invariance suppliers checked. Clause(a) uses existence of a locally integrable weak derivative as specified by D_j; it does not require global L2 derivative. Local L1 follows by Cauchy-Schwarz on bounded sets. Both inclusions in product-domain intersection checked; subtraction yields +i hbar f under first-variable linearity. Finite r and d>=1, hbar>0, zero f and Schwartz membership cause no endpoint/inverse issues. Choice assumptions inherited; products never extended beyond their actual domains.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the
cited scalar operator and spectral suppliers. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$. Let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the
component-valued space of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]
with its componentwise inner product, let $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$ be the
scalar position and momentum operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]], and let
$\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^{1}$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Write
$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}:=\Psi_{0}\bigl(\bigoplus_{l}\mathcal F_{2}\bigr)\Psi_{0}^{-1}$
for its componentwise version, with $\Psi_{0}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a).
Define, componentwise,
$$D(Q_{j}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (Q_{j}f)_{l}:=x_{j}f_{l},$$
$$D(P_{k}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ D_{k}f_{l}\text{ exists in }L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
where $D_{k}$ is the weak derivative of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]].
Write $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the classes whose components
lie in $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]),
and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the componentwise Schwartz
class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]). Then:

(a) under $\Psi_{0}$ the operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are the orthogonal sums
$\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]]; in particular
$Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are densely defined and self-adjoint with the displayed
domains;

(b) $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is unitary,
$$D(P_{k})=\bigl\{f\in H^{(r)}:\ \xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\bigr\},$$
and for every $f\in D(P_{k})$
$$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}(P_{k}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\,\xi_{k}\,\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi;$$

(c) the componentwise translation $T_{a}^{(r)}f:=f(\cdot-a)$, $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$,
is unitary, leaves $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$,
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$
invariant, satisfies $D_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)}f)=T_{a}^{(r)}(D_{k}f)$ for
$f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$, and
$$T_{a}^{(r)}D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=Q_{j}-a_{j}I,\qquad T_{a}^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(P_{k}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}P_{k}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=P_{k};$$

(d) for every $f\in D(P_{j})$,
$$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}f-f\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}f \qquad\text{in }H^{(r)},$$
so the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$t\mapsto T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}$ has generator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$ and
$$T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tP_{j}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the exponential being the spectral-calculus flow of the self-adjoint operator
$P_{j}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix integers $d\ge1$,
$r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$, let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the
component-valued space with the componentwise position and momentum operators
$Q_{j},P_{k}$ of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]
clauses (a) and (b), with domains
$$D(Q_{j})=\{f=(f_{l}):\ x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\},\qquad D(P_{k})=\{f=(f_{l}):\ D_{k}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\},$$
and let $D_{k}$ denote the weak partial derivative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]). Then:

(a) *Product rule.* If $f\in H^{(r)}$ has $x_{j}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$
and $x_{j}D_{j}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ (the latter read
componentwise), then $x_{j}f$ lies in $D(P_{j})$ and
$$D_{j}(x_{j}f)=f+x_{j}D_{j}f;$$

(b) *The product domain.* $D(Q_{j}P_{j})=\{f\in D(P_{j}):\ x_{j}D_{j}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\}$
and $D(P_{j}Q_{j})=\{f\in D(Q_{j}):\ D_{j}(x_{j}f)\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\}$,
and their intersection is
$$D(Q_{j}P_{j})\cap D(P_{j}Q_{j})=\bigl\{f\in H^{(r)}:\ D_{j}f,\ x_{j}f,\ x_{j}D_{j}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\bigr\};$$

(c) *Commutator identity.* For every $f\in D(Q_{j}P_{j})\cap D(P_{j}Q_{j})$,
$$(Q_{j}P_{j}-P_{j}Q_{j})f=i\hbar\,f;$$

(d) *Core.* The componentwise Schwartz class
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]])
is contained in $D(Q_{j}P_{j})\cap D(P_{j}Q_{j})$, and (c) holds on it.

No identity of unbounded products is asserted outside $D(Q_{j}P_{j})\cap D(P_{j}Q_{j})$;
in particular no identity is asserted on $D(P_{j})$ alone.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

derivations.claim: [The truncated vector] For $n\ge1$ put $\widetilde\varphi_{n}:=\chi_{n}(x_{j})\psi$, the componentwise product of the class $\psi$ with the bounded smooth function $\chi_{n}(x_{j})$. Since $|\chi_{n}|\le1$ and $\psi\in L^{2}$, the class $\widetilde\varphi_{n}\in H^{(r)}$ satisfies $\|\widetilde\varphi_{n}\|\le\|\psi\|$.

[Membership in the product domain] Since $\psi\in D(P_{j})$, [F1] with $\eta=\chi_{n}$ gives $D_{j}\widetilde\varphi_{n}=\chi_{n}'\psi+\chi_{n}D_{j}\psi$, a sum of two $L^{2}$ classes because $\chi_{n}'$ and $\chi_{n}$ are bounded; hence $\widetilde\varphi_{n}\in D(P_{j})$. Next $x_{j}D_{j}\widetilde\varphi_{n}=x_{j}\chi_{n}'\psi+x_{j}\chi_{n}D_{j}\psi$: the first summand is bounded in modulus by $C_{\chi}|\psi|$ pointwise by [F2], and the second by $2n|D_{j}\psi|$ because $|x_{j}\chi_{n}(x_{j})|\le2n$ on the support of $\chi_{n}$ and $D_{j}\psi\in L^{2}$ since $\psi\in D(P_{j})$; hence $x_{j}D_{j}\widetilde\varphi_{n}\in L^{2}$. Also $x_{j}\widetilde\varphi_{n}=x_{j}\chi_{n}\psi\in L^{2}$ because $|x_{j}\chi_{n}(x_{j})|\le2n$ is bounded. By [F4] the three memberships place $\widetilde\varphi_{n}$ in $D_{P}$.

[Convergence of the truncated sequence] As $n\to\infty$ one has $\chi_{n}(x_{j})\to1$, $\chi_{n}(x_{j})'\to0$ and $x_{j}\chi_{n}'(x_{j})\to0$ pointwise, with the uniform bounds $|\chi_{n}|\le1$, $|\chi_{n}'|\le\|\chi'\|_{\infty}/n$ and $|x_{j}\chi_{n}'|\le C_{\chi}$. Apply [F3] componentwise to the squared moduli: $|\chi_n\psi-\psi|^2\le|\psi|^2$ gives $\widetilde\varphi_n\to\psi$ in $H^{(r)}$, and $|x_j(\chi_n-1)\psi|^2\le|x_j\psi|^2$ gives $Q_j\widetilde\varphi_n\to Q_j\psi$. Both majorants are integrable by $\psi\in D(Q_j)$. For the momentum, $\|\chi_n'\psi\|_2\le\|\chi'\|_\infty\|\psi\|_2/n\to0$, while $| (\chi_n-1)D_j\psi|^2\le|D_j\psi|^2$ and pointwise convergence give $\chi_nD_j\psi\to D_j\psi$ in $L^2$ by [F3]; the last majorant is integrable because $\psi\in D(P_j)$. Therefore $$Q_{j}\widetilde\varphi_{n}=x_{j}\chi_{n}\psi\to x_{j}\psi=Q_{j}\psi,\qquad P_{j}\widetilde\varphi_{n}=-i\hbar\bigl(\chi_{n}'\psi+\chi_{n}D_{j}\psi\bigr)\to-i\hbar D_{j}\psi=P_{j}\psi$$ in $H^{(r)}$. In particular $\|\widetilde\varphi_{n}\|\to\|\psi\|>0$.

[Normalization] Since $\|\widetilde\varphi_{n}\|\to\|\psi\|>0$, choose $n_{0}$ such that $\widetilde\varphi_{n}\ne0$ for every $n\ge n_{0}$. Reindex this tail by setting $\varphi_{n}:=\widetilde\varphi_{n+n_{0}-1}/\|\widetilde\varphi_{n+n_{0}-1}\|$ for every $n\ge1$. Since $D_{P}$ is a linear subspace by [F4], $\varphi_{n}\in D_{P}$ and $\|\varphi_{n}\|=1$. Dividing the convergences of step 2.2 by $\|\widetilde\varphi_{n+n_{0}-1}\|\to\|\psi\|$ gives $\varphi_{n}\to\psi/\|\psi\|$, $Q_{j}\varphi_{n}\to Q_{j}\psi/\|\psi\|$ and $P_{j}\varphi_{n}\to P_{j}\psi/\|\psi\|$. If $\psi$ is a unit vector, these are the convergences $\varphi_{n}\to\psi$, $Q_{j}\varphi_{n}\to Q_{j}\psi$ and $P_{j}\varphi_{n}\to P_{j}\psi$.

[Means and second moments] Assume $\psi$ is a unit vector. By [F5], $\langle Q_{j}\varphi_{n},\varphi_{n}\rangle\to\langle Q_{j}\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|Q_{j}\varphi_{n}\|=\|Q_{j}\varphi_{n}-0\|\to\|Q_{j}\psi\|$ from the convergence $Q_{j}\varphi_{n}\to Q_{j}\psi$; the same two limits hold with $Q_{j}$ replaced by $P_{j}$. This completes the statement.

boundaries.reason: The statement fixes one nonzero class and constructs one sequence; no empty family or empty index set occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 normalizes only for $n$ with $\widetilde\varphi_{n}\ne0$, so the zero truncation is discarded rather than normalized.
Steps 1.1-4.1 are uniform in the coordinate $j$ and in $d$ and $r$, so $d=r=1$ is included.
Step 3.1 handles the finitely many vanishing truncations by discarding them, and step 4.1 uses only the nonzero unit approximants.

F2 gives chi_n=1 on [-n,n] and chi_n=0 outside [-2n,2n], with the uniform derivative bounds used in step 2.1. At each fixed coordinate, chi_n tends to 1 and its derivative tends to 0 as used in step 2.2; no zero limit outside the moving inner interval is asserted.

boundaries.reason: The explicit cutoff construction adds no choice use; AC and Countable Choice remain the stated hypotheses of the cited operator and convergence suppliers.
The lemma asserts exisence and convergence of a sequence, not an equivalence.
No converse statement is made; the lemma has no reverse direction.

risk_review.notes: All five steps checked against exact cutoff, weak Leibniz, product-domain and DCT statements. Cutoff only in coordinate j suffices: x_j chi_n bounded by 2n and x_j chi_n derivative bounded uniformly; no full spatial compact support required. Squared-modulus majorants |psi|^2, |x_j psi|^2 and |D_j psi|^2 are integrable. Derivative error <=||chi_prime|| ||psi||/n tends to zero. Nonzero psi ensures a tail with positive norms before normalization/reindexing. Graph convergence implies centered means/norm continuity; unit-vector specialization checked. No assertion of product convergence; no extra regularity or hidden choice.

citations.quote:
Adopt the postulates P1 and P2 ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]], [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]) and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(A,u_A)$ be an assigned sharp observable with outcome law $\mu^{A}$ in the reading of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]], and let $\rho$ be a preparation. Then:

(a) **Pure preparations.** Let $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ be the pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$. Then the mean of the outcome law exists and equals $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$, and the second moment exists and equals $\|A\psi\|^{2}$:
$$m(\psi)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^{2},$$
both read in the powers of the declared unit $u_A$ of the observable. If $\psi\in D(A^{2})$, the variance is
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(\lambda-m(\psi)\bigr)^{2}d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A^{2}\psi,\psi\rangle-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle^{2}.$$

(b) **Variance and its hypotheses.** For every unit $\psi\in D(A)$ the variance exists and equals
$$\operatorname{Var}_{\psi}(A)=\|A\psi\|^{2}-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle^{2}=\bigl\|(A-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle I)\psi\bigr\|^{2}\ge0,$$
without any hypothesis beyond $\psi\in D(A)$; no appeal to a discrete eigenbasis is made.

(c) **Non-existence is possible.** The identities of (a) and (b) are conditional on membership of $\psi$ in the stated domains. If $\psi\notin D(|A|^{1/2})$ then $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\infty$, so the mean of the outcome law does not exist as a finite real number; the mean is finite exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then $\psi$ need not lie in $D(A)$. If $\psi\notin D(A)$ then the second moment $\int\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}$ is infinite. In particular every preparation of the model is a unit ray or a density operator, and no preparation is equipped with finite moments automatically.

(d) **Mixtures.** Let $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ be a spectral expansion of a preparation, $w_n\ge0$, $\sum_nw_n=1$, $(u_n)$ orthonormal. In every weighted moment sum, zero-weight terms are defined to be zero before evaluating a component integral; equivalently, only positive-weight indices are summed. This applies also to component means that are undefined at zero-weight indices. Then the mean of $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is finite if and only if $\sum_nw_n\int|\lambda|\,dE_{A,u_n}<\infty$, and then $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}=\sum_nw_n\int\lambda\,dE_{A,u_n}$. For the second moment, put $M_n:=\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,u_n}$, so $M_n=\|Au_n\|^{2}$ for $u_n\in D(A)$ and $M_n=+\infty$ otherwise; a zero weight contributes zero. Then $\int\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}=\sum_nw_nM_n\in[0,\infty]$, and it is finite exactly when every $u_n$ of positive weight lies in $D(A)$ and $\sum_{n:w_n>0}w_n\|Au_n\|^{2}<\infty$. Thus componentwise domain membership alone does not guarantee a finite mixed-state second moment. Whenever the mixture has a finite absolute first moment, the identity of clause (b) of [[pthm-nrqm-observables-born-outcome-law-properties]] gives its mean as the absolutely convergent weighted average of the component means.

(e) **Status.** Clauses (a)-(d) are conditional consequences of P1 and P2 together with the mathematical moment results cited below; they assert no apparatus resolution, no measurement error, no disturbance and no empirical value. Whether a concrete preparation has a finite mean or variance for a concrete assigned observable is a question about the pair $(\rho,A)$ and the tested identification of the observable, not a consequence of the framework's postulates alone.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ and scalar measures $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). For a unit vector $\psi\in H$ write $\mu^{A}_{\psi}:=\mu^{A}_{T_{\psi,\psi}}$ for the scalar law of the pure state $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b). Then:

(a) **Second moment.** $\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^{2}$ if $\psi\in D(A)$, and the integral equals $+\infty$ if $\psi\notin D(A)$; thus the second moment of the scalar law is finite exactly on $D(A)$.

(b) **Mean.** $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ if and only if $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$; in that case the mean $m(\psi):=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)$ is finite and real, and if $\psi\in D(A)$ then $m(\psi)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$.

(c) **Variance.** If $\psi\in D(A)$ and $m:=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R}(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^{2}-m^{2}=\|(A-m)\psi\|^{2}\ge0 ;$$
if in addition $\psi\in D(A^{2})$, that is $\psi\in D(A)$ and $A\psi\in D(A)$, then $\|(A-m)\psi\|^{2}=\langle A^{2}\psi,\psi\rangle-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle^{2}$.

(d) **States.** Let $\rho$ be a density operator with expansion $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$, $w_n\ge0$, $\sum_nw_n=1$, $(u_n)$ orthonormal. In every weighted sum below, a term with $w_n=0$ is defined to be zero before any component integral is evaluated; equivalently, sum only over $n$ with $w_n>0$. This convention also applies to signed component means, which need not exist at zero-weight indices. Then for every Borel function $g\ge0$
$$\int_{\mathbb R}g\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}=\sum_nw_n\int_{\mathbb R}g\,dE_{A,u_n}\in[0,\infty],$$
so the mean of $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is finite if and only if $\sum_nw_n\int|\lambda|\,dE_{A,u_n}<\infty$, and then it equals $\sum_nw_n\int\lambda\,dE_{A,u_n}$. For the second moment, put $M_n:=\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,u_n}$, so $M_n=\|Au_n\|^{2}$ when $u_n\in D(A)$ and $M_n=+\infty$ otherwise; a zero weight contributes zero. Then $\int\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}=\sum_nw_nM_n\in[0,\infty]$. It is finite exactly when every $u_n$ with $w_n>0$ lies in $D(A)$ and $\sum_{n:w_n>0}w_n\|Au_n\|^{2}<\infty$; componentwise domain membership alone does not ensure a finite second moment.

**(a) Setting.** Adopt the state and composition postulate P1 and the
observable and probability postulate P2 in the readings of
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]] and
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]), and assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(A,u_{A})$ be an assigned sharp observable with
declared unit $u_{A}$ and outcome law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ in a preparation
$\rho$, in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b).

**(b) Preparation variance.** When the mean
$m(\rho):=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and the second
moment $\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ of the outcome
law are finite, the **preparation variance** of $(A,u_{A})$ in $\rho$ is
$$\operatorname{Var}_{\rho}(A):=\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(\lambda-m(\rho)\bigr)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda),$$
read in the square $u_{A}^{2}$ of the declared unit, and the **preparation
spread** is $\Delta_{\rho}A:=\operatorname{Var}_{\rho}(A)^{1/2}\ge0$, read in
the unit $u_{A}$. When either quantity is not finite the variance and the
spread of the pair in $\rho$ are **not defined**; the definition does not
extend them by $+\infty$.

**(c) Values and hypotheses.** The variance and its hypotheses are exactly
those of the moment theorem: for a pure preparation of a unit vector
$\psi\in D(A)$ the spread is $\Delta_{\psi}A=\|(A-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle I)\psi\|$,
equal to $\bigl(\langle A^{2}\psi,\psi\rangle-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$
when $\psi\in D(A^{2})$; for a preparation $\rho$ the identities and existence
criteria are those of [[pthm-nrqm-observables-preparation-moments]] and
[[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]]. In particular, for an orthonormal density expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_nT_{u_n,u_n}$, the mean is finite exactly when
$$\sum_{n:w_n>0}w_n\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,u_n}(\lambda)<\infty,$$
by [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]] clause (d); zero-weight
indices are omitted before evaluating their component integrals. For a pure
unit vector the corresponding criterion is membership in $D(|A|^{1/2})$
by clause (b). Componentwise domain membership alone does not imply
convergence of the weighted sum, and finite moments are not automatic.

**(d) Products of spreads.** For two assigned sharp observables $(A,u_{A})$
and $(B,u_{B})$ in a common preparation $\rho$ in which both spreads are
defined, the product $\Delta_{\rho}A\,\Delta_{\rho}B$ is a nonnegative real
number read in the product unit $u_{A}u_{B}$; for a pure preparation of a unit
vector in $D(A)\cap D(B)$ it is
$\|(A-a)\psi\|\,\|(B-b)\psi\|$ with the real means $a=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$
and $b=\langle B\psi,\psi\rangle$.

**(e) Reading and scope.** The spread $\Delta_{\rho}A$ is a property of the
pair (preparation, assigned observable): it is the standard deviation of the
outcome law that P2 assigns. It is not an apparatus resolution, not a
measurement error and not a disturbance of the preparation; those are further
objects that require a declared instrument or apparatus model and are not
introduced here. Clause (b) makes no claim that a preparation realizes a
specific laboratory state, that a laboratory procedure measures $A$ with
resolution $u_{A}$, or that the spread is observed in any experiment; the
identification of an apparatus with the pair $(A,u_{A})$ is a tested
identification under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7.
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] fixes the units in which the
displays are read.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A,B$ be symmetric
densely defined operators on $H$
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]), and let $u\in D(A)\cap D(B)$
with $\|u\|=1$ satisfy in addition $u\in D(AB)\cap D(BA)$, that is
$Bu\in D(A)$ and $Au\in D(B)$. Put
$$a:=\langle Au,u\rangle,\qquad b:=\langle Bu,u\rangle,\qquad x:=(A-a)u,\qquad y:=(B-b)u,\qquad \Delta A:=\|x\|,\qquad \Delta B:=\|y\|,$$
and write $\{A,B\}u:=ABu+BAu$ and $[A,B]u:=ABu-BAu$ for the pairings at $u$.
Then:

(a) $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $x,y\in H$, and
$$\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle=\tfrac12\bigl\langle\{(A-a),(B-b)\}u,u\bigr\rangle=\tfrac12\langle\{A,B\}u,u\rangle-ab, \qquad \langle[A,B]u,u\rangle=-2i\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle ;$$

(b) *(Robertson bound)* $\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\tfrac12\bigl|\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle\bigr|$;

(c) *(Schroedinger-Robertson bound)*
$$(\Delta A)^{2}(\Delta B)^{2}\ge\Bigl(\tfrac12\bigl\langle\{(A-a),(B-b)\}u,u\bigr\rangle\Bigr)^{2}+\tfrac14\bigl|\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle\bigr|^{2},$$
that is, with the expanded anticommutator pairing
$(\Delta A)^{2}(\Delta B)^{2}\ge\bigl(\tfrac12\langle\{A,B\}u,u\rangle-ab\bigr)^{2}+\tfrac14\bigl|\langle[A,B]u,u\rangle\bigr|^{2}$;
