Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

**(a) Adopted model and state space.** Adopt the kinematics and
massive-particle model postulate P5 for a declared particle of mass parameter
$m>0$, spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and internal factor
assigned as in the identical-particle and spin postulate P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]]). Put $r:=2s+1$ and take
as the model's one-particle state space the complex Hilbert space
$$H_{s}:=L^{2}\bigl(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r}\bigr) =\Bigl\{f:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb C^{r}\ \text{measurable}:\ \int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dx<\infty\Bigr\}\Big/\!\sim,$$
the quotient by equality almost everywhere, with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\sum_{l=1}^{r}f_{l}\overline{g_{l}}\,dx$
linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
Thus an element of $H_{s}$ is a class of functions, not a function, and
pointwise values of a state are not defined; the position density is read from
the class through the observables of clause (b) and the observable and
probability postulate P2 ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]],
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]). Its dimension
in the conventions of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)1
is $\ell^{-3/2}$ per component. P5 presents the same space as the completed
tensor product $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\widehat\otimes\mathbb C^{r}$
with the spin factor carrying the representation of P6; the unitary
identification of the two descriptions and the componentwise reading of
componentwise operators are those of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] and
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]. The orthonormal
basis $(e_{m})_{m=-s,\dots,s}$ of $\mathbb C^{r}$ is the basis fixed by P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii)).

**(b) Position and momentum.** The model's $j$-th position and $k$-th momentum
are the componentwise operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a): for
$f=(f_{l})$, restricted to the classes with $x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ respectively
with $D_{k}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ for all $l$,
$$(Q_{j}f)_{l}(x):=x_{j}f_{l}(x),\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
with $D_{k}$ the weak derivative and $\hbar$ the action constant of
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. These are the scalar operators of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]] applied
componentwise. The model assigns to $(Q_{j},\mathrm m)$ and to
$(P_{k},\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})$ the status of assigned sharp observables in
the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]
clause (a), with the units of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
clause (d)4; both are densely defined and self-adjoint by
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a). On the
Schwartz core they satisfy the componentwise canonical commutation relations,
and they commute with the internal-factor operators of clause (c) in the sense
of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]] clauses (a),(c).

**(c) Internal factor.** For $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ let $S_{i}=\hbar J_{i}$ be the
self-adjoint endomorphisms of $\mathbb C^{r}$ of the spin assignment P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii),
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]), and let the model read
them on $H_{s}$ as the matrix actions
$$(S_{i}f)_{l}:=\hbar\sum_{m=1}^{r}(J_{i})_{lm}f_{m}\qquad(l=1,\dots,r),$$
that is, as the amplifications $I\otimes S_{i}$ under the tensor
identification of clause (a) ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]]
clause (d)). Their declared unit is the unit of action ([[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
clause (d)4). The factor is internal bookkeeping: it is not a spatial
coordinate, not a rotating body and not a relativistic spinor, and the model
assigns no position or worldline to it.

**(d) Momentum-space representative.** With $U^{(s)}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] for $r=2s+1$, the
**momentum-space representative** of a preparation vector $\psi\in H_{s}$ is
$\psi_{p}:=U^{(s)}\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$; for a
Schwartz class $\psi$ it is the componentwise Fourier transform
$$(\psi_{p})_{l}(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi_{l}(x)\,dx,$$
and its dimension is $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})^{-3/2}$ per component
([[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)2). By
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] clause (b), $P_{k}$ acts on the
momentum representative by multiplication by $p_{k}$; this is the model's
momentum reading and no measured momentum distribution is identified with
$|\psi_{p}|^{2}$ by this definition.

**(e) Frame reading.** The model's inertial frames are the global coordinate
charts of P5; frame changes are the Galilean transformations of P5, with
parameters and units as in [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. This
definition uses P5's frame class only. For translations by $a\in\mathbb R^3$ and boosts with parameter $u\in\mathbb R^3$, choose the componentwise representative convention
$$(T_a\psi)(x)=\psi(x-a),\qquad (B_u(t)\psi)(x)=\exp\!\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}\left(mu\cdot x-\tfrac12m|u|^2t\right)\right)\psi(x-ut).$$
Here $a$ is length-valued, $u$ velocity-valued and $t$ time-valued, so the phase is dimensionless. These formulas specify classes almost everywhere and are chosen model conventions. The covariance theorems of this page derive operator and outcome-law identities conditional on these choices; they do not derive the choice of representative convention itself. No Lorentz transformation law is claimed.

**(f) Status.** Clauses (a)-(e) record the readings of P1, P2, P5 and P6 in the
terminology of this page and fix the objects used by its theorems. They assert
no time evolution beyond what the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4 assigns
([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]]
clause (iv)), no preparation or apparatus model, no detection model and no
empirical result. Massless particles, relativistic matter, radiation, singular
or unbounded potentials and boundary or confined realizations are separate
model assumptions with their own domains and self-adjointness statements; none
is obtained from this definition.

Adopt the postulates P1 and P2 ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]], [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]) and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(A,u_A)$ be an assigned sharp observable with outcome law $\mu^{A}$ in the reading of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]], and let $\rho$ be a preparation. Then:

(a) **Pure preparations.** Let $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ be the pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$. Then the mean of the outcome law exists and equals $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$, and the second moment exists and equals $\|A\psi\|^{2}$:
$$m(\psi)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^{2},$$
both read in the powers of the declared unit $u_A$ of the observable. If $\psi\in D(A^{2})$, the variance is
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(\lambda-m(\psi)\bigr)^{2}d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A^{2}\psi,\psi\rangle-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle^{2}.$$

(b) **Variance and its hypotheses.** For every unit $\psi\in D(A)$ the variance exists and equals
$$\operatorname{Var}_{\psi}(A)=\|A\psi\|^{2}-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle^{2}=\bigl\|(A-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle I)\psi\bigr\|^{2}\ge0,$$
without any hypothesis beyond $\psi\in D(A)$; no appeal to a discrete eigenbasis is made.

(c) **Non-existence is possible.** The identities of (a) and (b) are conditional on membership of $\psi$ in the stated domains. If $\psi\notin D(|A|^{1/2})$ then $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\lambda)=\infty$, so the mean of the outcome law does not exist as a finite real number; the mean is finite exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then $\psi$ need not lie in $D(A)$. If $\psi\notin D(A)$ then the second moment $\int\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\psi}$ is infinite. In particular every preparation of the model is a unit ray or a density operator, and no preparation is equipped with finite moments automatically.

(d) **Mixtures.** Let $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ be a spectral expansion of a preparation, $w_n\ge0$, $\sum_nw_n=1$, $(u_n)$ orthonormal. In every weighted moment sum, zero-weight terms are defined to be zero before evaluating a component integral; equivalently, only positive-weight indices are summed. This applies also to component means that are undefined at zero-weight indices. Then the mean of $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is finite if and only if $\sum_nw_n\int|\lambda|\,dE_{A,u_n}<\infty$, and then $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}=\sum_nw_n\int\lambda\,dE_{A,u_n}$. For the second moment, put $M_n:=\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,u_n}$, so $M_n=\|Au_n\|^{2}$ for $u_n\in D(A)$ and $M_n=+\infty$ otherwise; a zero weight contributes zero. Then $\int\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}=\sum_nw_nM_n\in[0,\infty]$, and it is finite exactly when every $u_n$ of positive weight lies in $D(A)$ and $\sum_{n:w_n>0}w_n\|Au_n\|^{2}<\infty$. Thus componentwise domain membership alone does not guarantee a finite mixed-state second moment. Whenever the mixture has a finite absolute first moment, the identity of clause (b) of [[pthm-nrqm-observables-born-outcome-law-properties]] gives its mean as the absolutely convergent weighted average of the component means.

(e) **Status.** Clauses (a)-(d) are conditional consequences of P1 and P2 together with the mathematical moment results cited below; they assert no apparatus resolution, no measurement error, no disturbance and no empirical value. Whether a concrete preparation has a finite mean or variance for a concrete assigned observable is a question about the pair $(\rho,A)$ and the tested identification of the observable, not a consequence of the framework's postulates alone.

**(a) Setting.** Adopt the state and composition postulate P1 and the
observable and probability postulate P2 in the readings of
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]] and
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]), and assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(A,u_{A})$ be an assigned sharp observable with
declared unit $u_{A}$ and outcome law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ in a preparation
$\rho$, in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b).

**(b) Preparation variance.** When the mean
$m(\rho):=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and the second
moment $\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ of the outcome
law are finite, the **preparation variance** of $(A,u_{A})$ in $\rho$ is
$$\operatorname{Var}_{\rho}(A):=\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(\lambda-m(\rho)\bigr)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda),$$
read in the square $u_{A}^{2}$ of the declared unit, and the **preparation
spread** is $\Delta_{\rho}A:=\operatorname{Var}_{\rho}(A)^{1/2}\ge0$, read in
the unit $u_{A}$. When either quantity is not finite the variance and the
spread of the pair in $\rho$ are **not defined**; the definition does not
extend them by $+\infty$.

**(c) Values and hypotheses.** The variance and its hypotheses are exactly
those of the moment theorem: for a pure preparation of a unit vector
$\psi\in D(A)$ the spread is $\Delta_{\psi}A=\|(A-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle I)\psi\|$,
equal to $\bigl(\langle A^{2}\psi,\psi\rangle-\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$
when $\psi\in D(A^{2})$; for a preparation $\rho$ the identities and existence
criteria are those of [[pthm-nrqm-observables-preparation-moments]] and
[[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]]. In particular, for an orthonormal density expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_nT_{u_n,u_n}$, the mean is finite exactly when
$$\sum_{n:w_n>0}w_n\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,u_n}(\lambda)<\infty,$$
by [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]] clause (d); zero-weight
indices are omitted before evaluating their component integrals. For a pure
unit vector the corresponding criterion is membership in $D(|A|^{1/2})$
by clause (b). Componentwise domain membership alone does not imply
convergence of the weighted sum, and finite moments are not automatic.

**(d) Products of spreads.** For two assigned sharp observables $(A,u_{A})$
and $(B,u_{B})$ in a common preparation $\rho$ in which both spreads are
defined, the product $\Delta_{\rho}A\,\Delta_{\rho}B$ is a nonnegative real
number read in the product unit $u_{A}u_{B}$; for a pure preparation of a unit
vector in $D(A)\cap D(B)$ it is
$\|(A-a)\psi\|\,\|(B-b)\psi\|$ with the real means $a=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$
and $b=\langle B\psi,\psi\rangle$.

**(e) Reading and scope.** The spread $\Delta_{\rho}A$ is a property of the
pair (preparation, assigned observable): it is the standard deviation of the
outcome law that P2 assigns. It is not an apparatus resolution, not a
measurement error and not a disturbance of the preparation; those are further
objects that require a declared instrument or apparatus model and are not
introduced here. Clause (b) makes no claim that a preparation realizes a
specific laboratory state, that a laboratory procedure measures $A$ with
resolution $u_{A}$, or that the spread is observed in any experiment; the
identification of an apparatus with the pair $(A,u_{A})$ is a tested
identification under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7.
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] fixes the units in which the
displays are read.

**(a) Assigned sharp observables.** Adopt the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) for a declared system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned sharp observable** of the system is a pair $(A,u_A)$ consisting of a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ on the assigned Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) and a **declared unit** $u_A$ in which the real spectral coordinate of $A$ is read, in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. The domain $D(A)$ is part of the assignment: symmetry on a smaller domain, or a formal differential expression, does not by itself supply an assigned observable ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Whether a concrete laboratory quantity of a given apparatus is described by a particular pair $(A,u_A)$ is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 and is not produced by this definition.

**(b) Spectral measure and outcome law.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral suppliers. The self-adjoint operator $A$ has a unique spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, with $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,x}<\infty\}$ and $Ax=\int\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)x$, where $E_{A,x}(B)=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$, that is a state $\rho\in D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], the **outcome law** of the pair $(A,u_A)$ in the preparation $\rho$ is the assignment
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_A(B)\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P2; for the pure preparation $[\psi]$ of a unit vector $\psi$ it is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$, which depends only on the ray by [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. The law is a probability measure on the Borel sets by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b), and it is affine in the preparation: for a statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\sum_nw_n\rho_n}=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-outcome-law-affinity-and-trace-norm-continuity]] clause (b).

**(c) Outcome sets and exact values.** A declared finite-resolution outcome of the quantity is a Borel set $B$; its probability in the preparation $\rho$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$, and a "value in $B$" is read only through this number. The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. In particular the model provides no normalizable eigenvector at a non-eigenvalue of $A$. If $A$ has no eigenvalues, every preparation has an atomless outcome law: each singleton has probability zero, while $\mathbb R$ remains the outcome space and the law is concentrated on $\sigma(A)$ as in clause (d). Zero singleton probability does not exclude real point values as realizations of this law; it supplies no normalized exact-value eigenstate. A finite-resolution record is read through its declared Borel bin, in the sense of clause (iii) of P2.

**(d) Spectral support.** The outcomes of the observable lie in its spectrum: with $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$ for every preparation by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable.

**(e) Moments.** The **mean** and the **variance** of the outcome law in a preparation are the numbers $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and $\int(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ with $m$ the mean, read in the declared unit $u_A$ and its square respectively; they exist only under the integrability hypotheses of [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]], which also supplies the formulas in terms of $A$ and the state. For a pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$ the mean and the second moment are $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|A\psi\|^{2}$; membership of $\psi$ in $D(A)$ or in $D(A^{2})$ is a genuine hypothesis and is not asserted for an arbitrary preparation.

**(f) Unsharp finite outcomes are separate.** Clause (iv) of P2 permits a finite family of bounded effects $F_a$ with $0\le F_a\le I$ and $\sum_aF_a=I$ and outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$ as an operational description of a finite-resolution apparatus. That extension is tied to an apparatus instrument and is developed, together with state updates, on the measurement-and-instruments page; this definition fixes only the sharp outcome law of clause (b) and makes no claim that every laboratory procedure realizes it.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the spectral theorem, assert no dynamics, no joint measurement of several observables, no detector realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by an assigned pair $(A,u_A)$. The additive additivity, support, atom and moment statements cited are mathematical consequences proved in the cited items; their physical reading is exactly the reading of P2 fixed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $E_{A,x}(B):=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ be its scalar measures ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ say that $\lambda$ is an **eigenvalue** of $A$ when $Ax=\lambda x$ for some nonzero $x\in D(A)$, the domain-restricted reading of [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]. Then:

(a) The orthogonal projection $E_A(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection of $H$ onto the eigenspace $\ker(A-\lambda)=\{x\in D(A):Ax=\lambda x\}$; in particular $E_A(\{\lambda\})\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.

(b) For every density operator $\rho$ on $H$, that is every self-adjoint positive trace-class $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)), the number $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(\{\lambda\}))$ is the weight that the scalar law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ assigns to the singleton $\{\lambda\}$: it vanishes for every $\rho$ whenever $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, and it equals $1$ for the pure state $T_{u,u}$ of every unit eigenvector $u\in\ker(A-\lambda)$.

(c) If $A$ has no eigenvalues at all, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=0$ for every density operator $\rho$ and every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: the scalar law of every state carries no point mass, while its values on general Borel sets remain $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(B))$.

Clauses (a)-(c) are mathematical statements about $A$, $E_A$ and the density operators; no physical interpretation of $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Adopt the state and composition postulate P1 and the observable and
probability postulate P2 in the readings of
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]] and
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]), and assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(A,u_{A})$ and $(B,u_{B})$ be assigned sharp
observables with outcome laws $\mu^{A},\mu^{B}$ and let
$\Delta_{\rho}A,\Delta_{\rho}B$ be their preparation spreads in the reading of
[[def-nrqm-uncertainty-preparation-spread]]. Let $\psi$ be a unit vector.
Whenever $\psi\in D(A)\cap D(B)$, put
$$a:=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad b:=\langle B\psi,\psi\rangle.$$
Then:

(a) **Weak form.** If $\psi\in D(A)\cap D(B)$, then the means $a,b$ are real,
the spreads $\Delta_{\psi}A$ and $\Delta_{\psi}B$ are defined, both are read in
the units $u_{A}$ and $u_{B}$, and
$$\Delta_{\psi}A\,\Delta_{\psi}B\ge\bigl|\operatorname{Im}\langle A\psi,B\psi\rangle\bigr| .$$

(b) **Robertson form.** If in addition $\psi\in D(AB)\cap D(BA)$, that is
$B\psi\in D(A)$ and $A\psi\in D(B)$, then the pairing
$\langle[A,B]\psi,\psi\rangle:=\langle AB\psi,\psi\rangle-\langle BA\psi,\psi\rangle$
is defined, is purely imaginary, and
$$\Delta_{\psi}A\,\Delta_{\psi}B\ge\tfrac12\bigl|\langle[A,B]\psi,\psi\rangle\bigr| ,$$
read in the product unit $u_{A}u_{B}$; moreover the anticommutator refinement
$$(\Delta_{\psi}A)^{2}(\Delta_{\psi}B)^{2}\ge\Bigl(\tfrac12\bigl\langle\{(A-a),(B-b)\}\psi,\psi\bigr\rangle\Bigr)^{2}+\tfrac14\bigl|\langle[A,B]\psi,\psi\rangle\bigr|^{2}$$
holds, with equality in the refined bound if and only if $(A-a)\psi$ and
$(B-b)\psi$ are linearly dependent.

(c) **Bounded observables.** If $A$ and $B$ are bounded everywhere-defined
self-adjoint operators, then clauses (a) and (b) hold for every unit
$\psi\in H$ with all hypotheses automatic ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

(d) **Status and scope.** Clauses (a)-(c) are conditional consequences of P1
and P2 and the cited mathematics. They concern the spreads of the two outcome
laws in one preparation; they introduce no joint outcome law, no apparatus
resolution, no measurement error, no disturbance of the preparation, and no
time observable. In particular no energy-time inequality is asserted, and
clauses (a)-(c) do not claim that a laboratory procedure realizes either
observable or attains the bounds; whether a concrete preparation and apparatus
realize the pair $(A,u_{A})$ and produce the spread $\Delta_{\psi}A$ is a
tested identification under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Adopt the state and composition postulate P1, the observable and probability
postulate P2 in the reading of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]], and the ideal
conditional measurement postulate P3 in the reading of
[[def-nrqm-measurement-framework-declared-measurements-and-instruments]]
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-ideal-conditional-measurement]]), and assume the Axiom
of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(A,u_{A})$ and $(B,u_{B})$ be assigned sharp
observables with spectral projection-valued measures $E_{A},E_{B}$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]],
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). Call a regular
projection-valued measure $H$ on the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^{2}$ a
**joint sharp observable** of the pair when its marginals are the two spectral
measures,
$$H(\Lambda\times\mathbb R)=E_{A}(\Lambda),\qquad H(\mathbb R\times\Sigma)=E_{B}(\Sigma)\qquad(\Lambda,\Sigma\ \text{Borel}),$$
and call the pair **compatible** when such an $H$ exists. Then:

(a) **Criterion.** The pair is compatible if and only if $A$ and $B$ strongly
commute in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-uncertainty-strong-spectral-commutation]] clause (b), if and only if
$f(A)g(B)=g(B)f(A)$ for all bounded Borel $f,g$; the joint sharp observable
$H$ is then unique, and for bounded Borel $f,g$
$$f(A)g(B)=\int_{\mathbb R^{2}}f(a)g(b)\,dH(a,b) .$$

(b) **Joint outcome law.** If the pair is compatible, then for every
preparation $\rho$ the assignment
$$\mu^{H}_{\rho}(S):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,H(S)\bigr)\qquad(S\subseteq\mathbb R^{2}\ \text{Borel})$$
is a probability measure on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R^{2}$, the **joint
outcome law** of the pair in $\rho$, and its marginals are the individual
laws:
$$\mu^{H}_{\rho}(\Lambda\times\mathbb R)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\Lambda),\qquad \mu^{H}_{\rho}(\mathbb R\times\Sigma)=\mu^{B}_{\rho}(\Sigma) .$$
For the pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi$ it reads
$\mu^{H}_{\psi}(S)=\|H(S)\psi\|^{2}$.

(c) **Ideal finite-resolution joint instrument.** If the pair is compatible
and $(P_{1},\dots,P_{n})$, $(Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m})$ are the projections of two
finite disjoint Borel partitions of $\mathbb R$,
$P_{i}:=E_{A}(\Lambda_{i})$, $Q_{j}:=E_{B}(\Sigma_{j})$ with
$\bigcup_{i}\Lambda_{i}=\bigcup_{j}\Sigma_{j}=\mathbb R$, then
$R_{ij}:=H(\Lambda_{i}\times\Sigma_{j})=P_{i}Q_{j}$ are mutually orthogonal
projections with strong sum $I$, and in the framework's declared ideal sharp
measurement of the family $(R_{ij})$ the outcome probabilities are
$\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})$ with marginals $\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_{i})$
and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho Q_{j})$. For each joint outcome $(i,j)$ with
$p_{ij}:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})>0$, the sequential declared ideal
measurements of $(P_{i})$ and then $(Q_{j})$, or in the reverse order, give the
same conditional state
$$\rho_{ij}=\frac{R_{ij}\rho R_{ij}}{p_{ij}}=\frac{Q_{j}P_{i}\rho P_{i}Q_{j}}{p_{ij}}=\frac{P_{i}Q_{j}\rho Q_{j}P_{i}}{p_{ij}}.$$
In that state an immediate repetition of the joint measurement or either
corresponding marginal-bin measurement returns the same outcome with
probability one. If $p_{ij}=0$, no conditional state or repeatability claim is
made for that outcome.

(d) **Scope.** Clauses (a)-(c) are conditional consequences of P1, P2, P3 and
the cited mathematics. A joint sharp observable, when it exists, is a
mathematical object of the framework: it supplies a joint outcome law, not an
apparatus. Clause (c)'s updates and repeatability are conditional ideal-model
claims under P3; no universal disturbance relation or apparatus-level
disturbance claim is asserted. The claim that a concrete laboratory device
realizes the joint measurement, with its resolution, losses and systematics, is
a physical identification with uncertainty under the preparation and
apparatus postulate P7. No dynamics or empirical result is asserted.

derivations.claim: [Spread identity] By [F1], $\sum_{i}S_{i}^{2}=\tfrac{3\hbar^{2}}{4}I$, so for a unit $\psi$, $$\sum_{i}\bigl(\Delta_{\psi}S_{i}\bigr)^{2}=\sum_{i}\langle S_{i}^{2}\psi,\psi\rangle-\sum_{i}\langle S_{i}\psi,\psi\rangle^{2}=\frac{3\hbar^{2}}{4}-\bigl|\langle\mathbf S\rangle_{\psi}\bigr|^{2}$$ by [F2]. This is the identity of (a).

[Noncommutation of the component projections] By [F3] the projections $P_{i}^{\pm}=E_{S_{i}}(\{\pm\hbar/2\})$ are the spectral projections of the components. Using $\sigma_{i}^{2}=I$ and $\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y}=i\sigma_{z}$, $\sigma_{y}\sigma_{x}=-i\sigma_{z}$ from [F1], $$P_{x}^{+}P_{y}^{+}-P_{y}^{+}P_{x}^{+}=\tfrac14(\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y}-\sigma_{y}\sigma_{x})=\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_{z}\ne0,$$ with nonzero action on any unit spatial factor times $e_{1/2}$. Cyclic permutations give nonvanishing differences for the other two pairs, so every two distinct components fail to strongly commute. If a joint sharp observable $H$ for components $i,j$ existed, [F6] applied to $\Lambda\times\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R\times\Sigma$ would give $E_{S_i}(\Lambda)E_{S_j}(\Sigma)=H(\Lambda\times\Sigma)=E_{S_j}(\Sigma)E_{S_i}(\Lambda)$ for all Borel sets, contradicting those projection witnesses. This proves (b) without an ideal-instrument assumption.

[Bound on the vector mean] Choose a representative of the class $\psi$ and write $g(x):=\bigl(\langle\sigma_{x}\psi(x),\psi(x)\rangle,\langle\sigma_{y}\psi(x),\psi(x)\rangle,\langle\sigma_{z}\psi(x),\psi(x)\rangle\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{3}$, which is defined for almost every $x$ and measurable. For $z=(z_{1},z_{2})\in\mathbb C^{2}$ the Pauli relations of [F1] give $\langle\sigma_{x}z,z\rangle=2\operatorname{Re}(z_{1}\overline{z_{2}})$, $\langle\sigma_{y}z,z\rangle=-2\operatorname{Im}(z_{1}\overline{z_{2}})$ and $\langle\sigma_{z}z,z\rangle=|z_{1}|^{2}-|z_{2}|^{2}$, hence the Bloch identity $\sum_{i}\langle\sigma_{i}z,z\rangle^{2}=4|z_{1}z_{2}|^{2}+(|z_{1}|^{2}-|z_{2}|^{2})^{2}=\|z\|^{4}$; so $|g(x)|=\|\psi(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{2}}^{2}$ for almost every $x$, and $g\in L^{1}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb R^{3})$ with $\|g\|_{1}=\|\psi\|^{2}=1$; and $\langle S_{i}\psi,\psi\rangle=\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}g_{i}(x)\,dx$ because $S_{i}$ acts on the internal factor. Put $M:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(x)\,dx$. If $M\ne0$, set $v:=M/|M|$; the real Cauchy-Schwarz inequality [F4] gives $|M|=v\cdot M=\int v\cdot g\le\int|g|$. If $M=0$, the same bound is immediate. Hence $$\bigl|\langle\mathbf S\rangle_{\psi}\bigr|=\frac{\hbar}{2}\Bigl|\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}g(x)\,dx\Bigr|\le\frac{\hbar}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}|g(x)|\,dx=\frac{\hbar}{2}.$$ Substituting into step 1.1 gives $\sum_{i}(\Delta_{\psi}S_{i})^{2}\ge\tfrac{3\hbar^{2}}{4}-\tfrac{\hbar^{2}}{4}=\tfrac{\hbar^{2}}{2}$; since the sum of the three nonnegative numbers is at least $\hbar^{2}/2$, their maximum is at least $\hbar^{2}/6$, so some component satisfies $\Delta_{\psi}S_{i}\ge\hbar/\sqrt6$. This completes (a).

[The $S_{z}$ eigenstate] Let $\psi=f\,e_{1/2}$ with $\|f\|=1$. Since $S_{i}$ acts on the internal factor, the pointwise expectations are constants: $\sigma_{z}e_{1/2}=e_{1/2}$ gives $\langle S_{z}\rangle_{\psi}=\tfrac{\hbar}{2}$, and $\sigma_{x}e_{1/2}=e_{-1/2}$, $\sigma_{y}e_{1/2}=ie_{-1/2}$ with the basis orthonormal give $\langle S_{x}\rangle_{\psi}=\langle S_{y}\rangle_{\psi}=0$. By [F1], $\langle S_{x}^{2}\rangle_{\psi}=\langle S_{y}^{2}\rangle_{\psi}=\tfrac{\hbar^{2}}{4}$, so $\Delta_{\psi}S_{x}=\Delta_{\psi}S_{y}=\hbar/2$; and $S_{z}\psi=\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\psi$ by the same eigenrelation, so $\Delta_{\psi}S_{z}=0$. Finally $[S_{x},S_{y}]=i\hbar S_{z}$ from [F1] gives $\tfrac12|\langle[S_{x},S_{y}]\psi,\psi\rangle|=\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\langle S_{z}\psi,\psi\rangle=\tfrac{\hbar^{2}}{4}=\Delta_{\psi}S_{x}\Delta_{\psi}S_{y}$, so the Robertson bound of [F5] is attained. This is (c).

[Scope] Clauses (a)-(c) used the internal matrices, the spread definition, the spectral-projection criterion and the Robertson relation; no measurement procedure, apparatus, dynamics or empirical input entered, which is the scope statement (d).

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<L<\infty$ and $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$. Put
$D_\theta:=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(L)=e^{i\theta}u^*(0)\},\qquad
P_\theta u:=-i\,Du,$
with $H^1$ and the trace $u^*$ of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]
and [[lem-nrqm-intervals-integration-by-parts]] clause (b). Then:

(a) $D_\theta$ is dense in $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, $P_\theta$ is symmetric and
self-adjoint;

(b) the functions
$\varphi_n(x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt L}e^{i(2\pi n+\theta)x/L}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z)$
form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, each
$\varphi_n\in D_\theta$, and $P_\theta\varphi_n=\kappa_n\varphi_n$ with
$\kappa_n:=\frac{2\pi n+\theta}{L};$
the eigenvalues $\kappa_n$ are simple and
$\sigma(P_\theta)=\{\kappa_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$;

(c) $P_\theta$ is the unique self-adjoint extension of the symmetric operator
$P_\theta$ restricted to the finite linear span of the $\varphi_n$, and its
domain is exactly
$D_\theta=\Bigl\{\sum_nc_n\varphi_n:\sum_n\kappa_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix complex
scalars. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, bounded or
unbounded, and write $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$ for the complex Hilbert space of
Lebesgue (equivalence classes of) square-integrable functions with the inner
product $\langle u,v\rangle=\int_Iu\overline v$ linear in the first argument
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**First-order space.** Define
$H^1(I):=\{u\in L^2(I;\mathbb C):\ \text{the weak derivative }Du\text{ of the class }u\text{ exists and }Du\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)\},$
where $Du$ is the weak derivative of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]: a class
$Du\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(I;\mathbb C)$ with
$\int_Iu\,\varphi'=(-1)\int_I(Du)\varphi\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(I),$
an identity that is choice-free
([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]). Equip
$H^1(I)$ with the sesquilinear form
$\langle u,v\rangle_{H^1}:=\int_Iu\overline v+\int_I(Du)\overline{Dv},$
whose associated norm is $\|u\|_{H^1}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$;
the symbol $u'$ denotes the same weak derivative $Du$ throughout the page.

**Second-order space.** Define
$H^2(I):=\{u\in H^1(I):Du\in H^1(I)\},$
and for $u\in H^2(I)$ write $D^2u:=D(Du)\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)$; the norm is
$\|u\|_{H^2}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2+\|D^2u\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$.
Thus $H^2(I)$ consists exactly of the classes in $L^2(I)$ whose first and
second weak derivatives exist and lie in $L^2(I)$, and $H^2(I)\subseteq
H^1(I)$.

**Endpoint-vanishing first-order space and the Dirichlet form.** For the
bounded interval $(0,L)$, $L>0$, define
$H^1_0(0,L):=\overline{C_c^\infty(0,L)}^{\,\|\cdot\|_{H^1}},$
the closure of the test functions in $H^1(0,L)$, and define the **Dirichlet
form** on it by $q_D[u]:=\|Du\|_{L^2(0,L)}^2=\int_0^L|Du|^2$.

**Elementary consequences, recorded for reuse.** Weak derivatives are unique
as locally integrable classes under Countable Choice, are additive and
$\mathbb C$-homogeneous, and classical derivatives of continuously
differentiable functions are weak derivatives. The cited published items
supply these facts, so $H^1(I)$ and $H^2(I)$ are well-defined linear
subspaces of $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$. No claim is made here that $H^1_0(0,L)$
equals the set of classes with vanishing endpoint values; that identification
is proved on this page from the trace estimates.

Assume the Axioms of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]).
Use the spaces of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]] and the
absolutely continuous representatives supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-intervals-weak-derivative-ac-representative]].

(a) *Bounded intervals.* Let $0<L<\infty$ and $u,v\in H^1(0,L)$. Then
$\int_0^Lu\,\overline{v'}=u^*(L)\overline{v^*(L)}-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}
-\int_0^Lu'\,\overline v .$

(b) *Endpoint-vanishing space.* $H^1_0(0,L)=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(0)=u^*(L)=0\}$,
with the traces $u^*(0),u^*(L)$ of the continuous representative.

(c) *Second-order identity.* For $u,v\in H^2(0,L)$,
$\int_0^L\bigl(u''\overline v-u\,\overline{v''}\bigr)
=\bigl[u'^*\overline{v^*}-u^*\overline{v'^*}\bigr]_0^L,$
where the bracket denotes
$u'^*(L)\overline{v^*(L)}-u^*(L)\overline{v'^*(L)}
-u'^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}+u^*(0)\overline{v'^*(0)}$.

(d) *Half-line and line.* If $u,v\in H^1(0,\infty)$, then
$\int_0^\infty u\overline{v'}=-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}-\int_0^\infty u'\overline v$, both integrals
being absolutely convergent. For $u,v\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ one instead has
$\int_{\mathbb R}u\overline{v'}=-\int_{\mathbb R}u'\overline v$,
with both integrals absolutely convergent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $E_{A,x}(B):=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ be its scalar measures ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ say that $\lambda$ is an **eigenvalue** of $A$ when $Ax=\lambda x$ for some nonzero $x\in D(A)$, the domain-restricted reading of [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]. Then:

(a) The orthogonal projection $E_A(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection of $H$ onto the eigenspace $\ker(A-\lambda)=\{x\in D(A):Ax=\lambda x\}$; in particular $E_A(\{\lambda\})\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.

(b) For every density operator $\rho$ on $H$, that is every self-adjoint positive trace-class $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)), the number $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(\{\lambda\}))$ is the weight that the scalar law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ assigns to the singleton $\{\lambda\}$: it vanishes for every $\rho$ whenever $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, and it equals $1$ for the pure state $T_{u,u}$ of every unit eigenvector $u\in\ker(A-\lambda)$.

(c) If $A$ has no eigenvalues at all, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=0$ for every density operator $\rho$ and every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: the scalar law of every state carries no point mass, while its values on general Borel sets remain $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(B))$.

Clauses (a)-(c) are mathematical statements about $A$, $E_A$ and the density operators; no physical interpretation of $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**The scope is exactly the continuous case, and that is not a limitation of the
proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion
page.

derivations.claim: [The hypothesis of the refuted statement holds] By [F2], $D\subseteq D_{0}\cap D_{\pi}=D(A)\cap D(B)$, and both operators act on $D$ by $u\mapsto-iDu$, which maps $D$ into itself; hence for $u\in D$ the products $ABu=-D^{2}u$ and $BAu=-D^{2}u$ are defined and $[A,B]u=0$. By [F3] the space $D$ is dense in $H$. So the hypotheses of the refuted statement are satisfied.

[Spectral data] Applying [F1] with $L=1$: $A=P_{0}$ has the complete orthonormal family $\varphi_{n}(x)=e^{2\pi inx}$ with simple eigenvalues $2\pi n$, and $B=P_{\pi}$ has the complete orthonormal family $\psi_{n}(x)=e^{i(2n+1)\pi x}$ with simple eigenvalues $(2n+1)\pi$, for $n\in\mathbb Z$. In particular $\varphi_{0}=1$ spans the eigenspace of $A$ at $0$ and $\psi_{0}(x)=e^{i\pi x}$ spans the eigenspace of $B$ at $\pi$.

[The two spectral projections] By [F4], $E_{A}(\{0\})$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb C\varphi_{0}$, and $E_{B}(\{\pi\})$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb C\psi_{0}$. Since $\varphi_{0}=1$ is a unit vector, $E_{A}(\{0\})u=\langle u,\varphi_{0}\rangle\varphi_{0}$; since $\|\psi_{0}\|^{2}=\int_{0}^{1}|e^{i\pi x}|^{2}dx=1$, likewise $E_{B}(\{\pi\})u=\langle u,\psi_{0}\rangle\psi_{0}$.

[The inner products] By [F5], $\int_{0}^{1}e^{-i\pi x}dx=\bigl[e^{-i\pi x}/(-i\pi)\bigr]_{0}^{1}=(e^{-i\pi}-1)/(-i\pi)=2/(i\pi)=-2i/\pi$, and by conjugation $\int_{0}^{1}e^{i\pi x}dx=2i/\pi$. Hence $\langle\varphi_{0},\psi_{0}\rangle=-2i/\pi$ and $\langle\psi_{0},\varphi_{0}\rangle=2i/\pi$.

[Noncommutation] With $u:=\varphi_{0}=1$ and the projections of step 2.1, $$E_{B}(\{\pi\})u=\langle u,\psi_{0}\rangle\psi_{0}=-\frac{2i}{\pi}\psi_{0},\qquad E_{A}(\{0\})E_{B}(\{\pi\})u=\langle u,\psi_{0}\rangle\langle\psi_{0},u\rangle u=\Bigl(\frac{2}{\pi}\Bigr)^{2}u,$$ because $\langle\psi_{0},u\rangle=\overline{\langle u,\psi_{0}\rangle}=2i/\pi$, so the product of the two coefficients is $(-2i/\pi)(2i/\pi)=4/\pi^{2}$. Thus $E_{A}(\{0\})E_{B}(\{\pi\})u=(4/\pi^{2})u$ while $E_{B}(\{\pi\})E_{A}(\{0\})u=E_{B}(\{\pi\})u=-(2i/\pi)\psi_{0}$. The vectors $u=1$ and $\psi_{0}=e^{i\pi x}$ are linearly independent in $L^{2}(0,1;\mathbb C)$ (the continuous function $e^{i\pi x}$ is not constant on $(0,1)$), so the two results differ. Therefore $E_{A}(\{0\})E_{B}(\{\pi\})\ne E_{B}(\{\pi\})E_{A}(\{0\})$: the spectral projection-valued measures of $A$ and $B$ do not strongly commute, and the refuted statement fails for this pair.
